design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover human laboratory study in an outpatient research unit (New York State Psychiatric Institute). Thirteen men who used methamphetamine recreationally completed five 2-day blocks (10 sessions). Day 1 of each block was a sample session: one intranasal amphetamine condition (placebo, or methamphetamine or d-amphetamine at 12 or 50 mg/70 kg, as study conditions) plus a monetary reinforcer (US$5 for 7 participants, US$20 for 6). Day 2 was a choice session in which participants worked on a progressive response schedule for portions of the sampled drug or the sampled money. Plasma amphetamine levels, cardiovascular measures, visual-analogue mood ratings, a drug-effect questionnaire and two psychomotor tasks were measured before and repeatedly after dosing, and again 24 h later as residual effects.
can_establish: Within these 13 experienced men, whether the two amphetamines, at the two tested dose levels and by the intranasal route, differed in how often each was chosen over money and in acute mood, cardiovascular and psychomotor measures; and how an alternative monetary reinforcer of $5 versus $20 changed drug choice.
cannot_establish: Whether methamphetamine and d-amphetamine differ in abuse potential outside this setting (choice was between a drug portion and money during a 4-hour working day, in people with methamphetamine but not necessarily d-amphetamine experience); whether the drugs differ at other dose levels, by other routes, in women, or in people without amphetamine experience; or whether any observed drug difference reflects pharmacology rather than familiarity with methamphetamine's effects. The $5-versus-$20 contrast is between participants (7 vs 6), not within.

sample.recruitment: Advertisement and word of mouth: word-of-mouth referral and newspaper and online advertisements in New York City; outpatient; paid $60 per day and debriefed about conditions at discharge (Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men who currently used methamphetamine; passed medical examination and psychiatric interview; within normal weight range by the 1983 Metropolitan Life tables; not seeking treatment; no other Axis I disorder. Three met criteria for current methamphetamine dependence; the diagnostic system is not named in the text. No women were enrolled and no reason is given. Other exclusion criteria are not listed.
sample.demographics: 13 men (1 Asian, 6 Black, 2 Hispanic, 4 White); mean age 37.4 years (SD 7.3); education 14.8 years (SD 2.0); BMI 24.9 (SD 2.7) (Methods › Participants).
sample.attrition: Not reported: the paper describes 13 completers and says nothing about enrolment, withdrawal or missing sessions.
sample.selection_effects: Advertisement-recruited, medically and psychiatrically screened men who used methamphetamine about 9 days a month, mostly without dependence (3 of 13), not seeking treatment, and already familiar with methamphetamine's effects but with no reported d-amphetamine experience. This asymmetry of experience sits directly on the study's comparison. Men only, so no data on women. Outpatient design means behaviour outside sessions was not controlled.

exposure.measurement: Experimental administration of methamphetamine HCl (supplied by NIDA) or d-amphetamine sulfate (Cambrex), prepared by the institute pharmacy with lactose as placebo and filler, double-blind; plasma amphetamine levels measured from an intravenous line at baseline and 15, 60, 90, 120, 180 and 240 min. Participants' own use was self-reported. Before each session participants passed a field sobriety test and gave a urine sample required to be negative for several drug metabolites, with amphetamines and THC excluded from that requirement (Methods › Procedure).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: single intranasal doses of 0, 12 or 50 mg/70 kg of methamphetamine or of d-amphetamine on day 1 of each block, with blocks at least 48 h apart and condition order counterbalanced across participants; on day 2 participants could earn up to the same total amount in ten 10% portions. Participants' own reported use: methamphetamine on 9.4 (SD 4.7) days per month. Comparison with real-world patterns: the authors note that choice in this study occurred in the morning before a 4-hour period of computerized tasks, unlike recreational use, and that use outside the laboratory may occur in the evening in social settings (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Current use reported by participants: alcohol 7 of 13 (4 to 10 drinks a week), cocaine 7 of 13 (1 to 8 days a month), cannabis 3 of 13 (4 to 12 days a month), tobacco 4 of 13 (3 to 20 cigarettes a day). Handled only by pre-session sobriety testing and urine screens that did not include amphetamines or THC; this was an outpatient study, and the authors name undetected outside drug use as a limitation for the 24-hour residual findings (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Same-day abstinence only, checked by field sobriety test and a urine screen that excluded amphetamines and THC from the negativity requirement. No washout beyond the 48 h between blocks; the 24-hour measures are explicitly residual-effect measures taken the morning after dosing.

comparison.controls: Two within-participant comparators: placebo, and the other amphetamine at the matched dose level. Each participant experienced all five conditions.
comparison.matching: Within-participant for drug and dose; condition order counterbalanced (sequences not reported). The monetary reinforcer magnitude ($5 vs $20) was a between-participant factor with 7 and 6 participants, not matched or randomized by any reported procedure, and the two groups are compared only on drug choice (the paper states they did not differ on physiological, subjective or performance measures, without giving those tests).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to within-person contrasts. The relevant unmeasured variables are prior d-amphetamine experience (not reported for any participant), expectancy (all had received the 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine condition openly before the study), and tolerance to methamphetamine but not to d-amphetamine.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants across conditions; see polysubstance.

outcomes.instruments: Self-administration: computerized 50-min choice task with 10 trials, response requirements rising from 50 to 2800 finger presses per trial (11,550 responses to obtain the full reinforcer); outcome is the number of drug options chosen out of 10. Plasma amphetamine. Heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure at baseline and 5, 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240 min. Computerized 100-mm visual-analogue mood scales at the same times, summed across the session (maximum 700). Drug-effect questionnaire at 45 min (good effects, bad effects, strength, desire to take the drug again on 0 to 4; liking on -4 to +4). Psychomotor battery: digit-symbol substitution task and divided attention task. Residual measures: the same subjective, cardiovascular and performance measures at baseline on the choice day, about 24 h after dosing (Methods › Procedure; Subjective-Effects and Psychomotor Battery).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard human-laboratory abuse-liability measures; within-person contrasts, so norms are not required. Participants were trained on the tasks in two 3 to 4 h sessions before the study.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Abuse potential' was operationalized as the number of drug options chosen over money on the progressive-response choice task, plus positive subjective ratings. 'Equivalence' of the two drugs was inferred from non-significant between-drug comparisons, not from an equivalence test or a prespecified margin.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: all tests at p<0.05 with Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity where appropriate. The count is a lower bound: the VAS item list is given by example only, Table 2 shows 13 items, and the drug-effect questionnaire, cardiovascular, plasma, choice and two performance tasks add further measures, each tested acutely and again at 24 h.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind administration; blinding integrity not assessed, and participants were experienced with methamphetamine only. Outcomes are self-rated, automated or computerized.

analysis.effect_sizes: The paper reports p values, summed-rating means with SEM (Table 2) and figures; no F statistics for most analyses, no effect sizes and no confidence intervals. Choice data analysed by single-factor repeated-measures ANOVA separately in the $5 (n=7) and $20 (n=6) groups; sample-session cardiovascular, plasma and performance data by two-factor (condition x time) ANOVA; subjective ratings summed across the session and analysed by single-factor ANOVA; residual measures by single-factor ANOVA. Editors' calculation from Table 2 (SD = SEM x square root of 13, difference divided by the average of the two SDs, ignoring the within-person correlation, so approximate): summed 'high' and 'good drug effect' are not in Table 2; for drug-effect-questionnaire 'good drug effect' (0 to 4), 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine vs placebo d about 2.3 and vs the matched d-amphetamine condition about 0.6; for summed 'stimulated', methamphetamine vs placebo about 1.1 and vs matched d-amphetamine about 0.5. These are indicative only. Key quantitative statements the paper does give: overall drug choice 41% under $5 versus 17% under $20; roughly 47 to 50% drug choice for either amphetamine at the larger dose under $5; 24-hour heart rate 76.8 (SEM 2.3) bpm after placebo versus 86.1 (1.9) after 12 mg/70 kg methamphetamine, 87.8 (2.3) after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine and 90.5 (3.4) after 50 mg/70 kg d-amphetamine.
analysis.covariates: None. No adjustment for period or for the between-group difference in monetary reinforcer in the pooled analyses.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. The paper states two directional hypotheses in the Introduction (equal self-administration under $5, attenuation under $20; dose-dependent increases in positive ratings, cardiovascular values and performance).
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 2 lists only items with statistically significant effects, so the full VAS item set and its null results are unavailable; 'bad effects' from the drug-effect questionnaire is described in Methods but not reported anywhere. Figures 1 to 4 carry the plasma, cardiovascular, choice and performance values, which cannot be read as numbers. The statement that the $5 and $20 groups did not differ on any physiological, subjective or performance measure is given without the tests. Subjective ratings were analysed as session sums, which is not the same analysis used in the companion single-drug study.
analysis.power: Not reported. n=13 overall and 7 and 6 for the two choice analyses. The central claim (no difference between the drugs in self-administration) rests on non-significant tests in groups of 7 and 6, which cannot exclude a substantial difference; no equivalence margin was set.

interpretation_gap.results_show: With $5 as the alternative, both amphetamines at 50 mg/70 kg were chosen more often than placebo (n=7); with $20 as the alternative, money was chosen almost always and no dose effect appeared (n=6); overall 41% of choices were for drug under $5 versus 17% under $20. No significant difference between methamphetamine and d-amphetamine in number of drug choices. Both drugs raised plasma levels dose-dependently (peak 3 to 4 h) and raised heart rate and blood pressure at 50 mg/70 kg (peak within 15 min), with heart rate higher under methamphetamine. Summed ratings of alert, energetic, friendly, social, stimulated, talkative and nose burning rose and sleepy and tired fell at the larger doses of both drugs; at the matched larger dose, methamphetamine exceeded d-amphetamine on 'high', 'stimulated', heart pounding, drug-effect-questionnaire good drug effect and drug strength. At 24 h, heart rate remained above placebo after both 50 mg/70 kg conditions and after 12 mg/70 kg methamphetamine, diastolic pressure after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine, and ratings of 'content' were lower after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine than after every other condition. Both drugs raised maximum tracking speed on the divided attention task; only the smaller doses shortened hit latency; no digit-symbol effects.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the drugs were self-administered equally, "indicating their equivalence for abuse potential", and the discussion states the data do not support the view that methamphetamine is a more potent reinforcer in humans. Gaps: (1) equivalence is inferred from non-significant tests in 7 and 6 participants with no equivalence margin, which is absence of evidence rather than evidence of equivalence; (2) participants were experienced with methamphetamine and no d-amphetamine experience is reported, an asymmetry the authors themselves raise for the subjective findings but not for the choice findings; (3) the abstract reports no significant differences on most measures while the same results show methamphetamine higher on several mood items, heart rate, drug strength and 24-hour 'content'; (4) the conclusion that methamphetamine use is likely influenced by non-pharmacological factors is an inference about population patterns from a 13-man laboratory choice task; (5) the 41% versus 17% contrast is between two small non-randomized groups.

timeline.event: Martin et al.: oral methamphetamine and d-amphetamine produced overlapping physiological and subjective effects (cited in this paper's Introduction).
Lamb and Henningfield: humans trained to discriminate d-amphetamine generalized to methamphetamine (cited in Introduction).
Sevak et al.: methamphetamine, d-amphetamine and methylphenidate produced similar discriminative-stimulus and subject-rated effects in people trained on methamphetamine (cited in Introduction).
This study: first direct comparison of the two amphetamines by a route associated with non-medical use, and the first with a self-administration endpoint.

replication.where_it_stands: The only direct human self-administration comparison of the two amphetamines found in this reading, with 13 men and 6 to 7 per choice group. Its finding of no difference in choice agrees in direction with animal self-administration work cited by the authors (Balster and Schuster 1973; Yokel and Pickens 1973) and with oral human comparisons, but the sample cannot exclude a moderate difference, and the single-drug intranasal dose-response data come from the same laboratory (Hart et al., 2008).

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA-19559 to Dr Hart (Acknowledgements). Study methamphetamine supplied by NIDA; d-amphetamine supplied by Cambrex (Methods › Drug).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that apart from income from their primary employer they received no financial support or compensation from any individual or corporate entity in the past 3 years for research or professional service, hold no personal financial holdings that could be perceived as a conflict, and had no constraints on publishing the data (Declaration of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at Columbia University and the New York State Psychiatric Institute (Division on Substance Abuse), with one author at Wayne State University. Cambrex supplied d-amphetamine as a material donation only. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A larger crossover self-administration study with a within-participant manipulation of the alternative reinforcer, a prespecified equivalence margin, participants with comparable prior experience of both amphetamines (or a sample with experience of neither), both sexes, and a choice context closer to real-world settings, would show whether the two amphetamines are genuinely equal in reinforcing efficacy rather than only not distinguishable in a small sample.

domains.note: Described as randomized and counterbalanced, but the sequence-generation and concealment methods are not described, and the $5 versus $20 assignment (7 vs 6 participants) is not stated to be randomized.

Blocks were separated by at least 48 h, yet the paper itself shows effects persisting at 24 h (heart rate, diastolic pressure, 'content'), so carryover into the next block cannot be excluded; period was not modelled; the example design in Table 1 shows both methamphetamine conditions in week 1 and both d-amphetamine conditions in week 2, with placebo last.

Double-blind in form, but all participants had received the 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine condition openly before the study, all were experienced with methamphetamine and none is reported to have used d-amphetamine; blinding integrity was not assessed. Outpatient setting with no control of behaviour between sessions.
Only 13 completers are described; enrolment, withdrawals and missing sessions are not reported.

Choice and performance are computerized and cardiovascular measures automated (low concern), but the main subjective outcomes are self-ratings by participants who may have recognized their familiar drug.

No protocol or registration; only significant VAS items tabulated; 'bad effects' collected but never reported; between-group equivalence of the $5 and $20 groups asserted without tests; subjective data analysed as session sums without a stated plan.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The within-person dose-response findings (both drugs raised plasma levels, cardiovascular measures and positive ratings) are robust to these concerns. The headline comparative conclusion is not: it rests on non-significant differences in 6 to 7 participants per choice group, in people experienced with one of the two drugs but not reported as experienced with the other, without an equivalence margin, with possible carryover given the documented 24-hour residual effects, and with selective tabulation of outcomes.

key_findings.finding: Participants: 13 men, mean age 37.4 (SD 7.3), education 14.8 years (SD 2.0), using methamphetamine 9.4 (SD 4.7) days a month; 3 met criteria for current methamphetamine dependence; none sought treatment; no other Axis I disorder. No women enrolled; no prior d-amphetamine use is reported.

Design: 5 two-day blocks at least 48 h apart; day 1 sample session with one of 5 conditions (placebo; methamphetamine or d-amphetamine at 12 or 50 mg/70 kg as study conditions) plus $5 (7 participants) or $20 (6 participants); day 2 choice session with 10 trials for 10% portions of drug or money, response requirement rising from 50 to 2800 presses (11,550 for the full reinforcer).
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials › Design; Procedure › Choice (self-administration) sessions; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Before the study each participant received the 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine condition openly in a familiarization session; no untoward effects were noted.

Self-administration with $5 as the alternative (n=7): both drugs at 50 mg/70 kg were chosen more often than placebo (p<0.05), with no significant difference between methamphetamine and d-amphetamine; the discussion gives roughly 47 to 50% drug choice for either drug at that dose level. With $20 as the alternative (n=6), money was chosen almost always and no dose effect was significant. Overall drug choices: 41% under $5 versus 17% under $20.
key_findings.locator: Results › Methamphetamine and d-Amphetamine Choice; Figure 2; Abstract › Findings; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The 41% vs 17% comparison is between two small non-randomized groups and no test is reported for it. Choice counts appear only in Figure 2 (image).

key_findings.finding: Plasma concentrations of both drugs rose dose-dependently, with peaks 3 to 4 h after dosing; every active condition exceeded placebo and each 50 mg/70 kg condition exceeded the matched 12 mg/70 kg condition (p<0.0001). Values appear only in Figure 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Plasma Methamphetamine and d-Amphetamine Levels; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Both 50 mg/70 kg conditions raised heart rate and systolic and diastolic pressure above placebo and above the 12 mg/70 kg conditions (p<0.01), with peaks within 15 min; methamphetamine raised heart rate more than d-amphetamine (p<0.05). Magnitudes appear only in Figure 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular Effects › Acute Effects; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Residual cardiovascular effects at about 24 h: heart rate (mean, SEM) 76.8 (2.3) bpm after placebo versus 86.1 (1.9) after 12 mg/70 kg methamphetamine, 87.8 (2.3) after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine and 90.5 (3.4) after 50 mg/70 kg d-amphetamine (p<0.01); diastolic pressure 74.4 (2.2) versus 78.4 (2.4) mmHg after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine (p<0.05).
key_findings.note: Outpatient design: the authors note undetected drug use between sessions could contribute. The 12 mg/70 kg d-amphetamine condition is absent from the list of significant comparisons.

key_findings.finding: Summed visual-analogue ratings (maximum 700), placebo / 12 mg AMPH / 12 mg MA / 50 mg AMPH / 50 mg MA: energetic 271 / 319 / 361 / 414 / 468; stimulated 111 / 160 / 172 / 226 / 320; social 314 / 346 / 367 / 448 / 454; nose burning 37 / 48 / 41 / 102 / 107; heart pounding 26 / 24 / 19 / 29 / 66; sleepy 205 / 163 / 88 / 67 / 47; tired 224 / 176 / 127 / 68 / 56. Methamphetamine at 50 mg/70 kg exceeded the matched d-amphetamine condition on stimulated and heart pounding.

Drug-effect questionnaire (0 to 4 scale; liking -4 to +4), placebo / 12 mg AMPH / 12 mg MA / 50 mg AMPH / 50 mg MA: good drug effect 0.7 / 0.8 / 1.6 / 2.3 / 3.1; like drug -0.1 / 0.7 / 1.1 / 2.1 / 2.8; drug strength 1.1 / 1.0 / 1.7 / 2.5 / 3.1. Methamphetamine at 50 mg/70 kg exceeded the matched d-amphetamine condition on good drug effect and drug strength; both drugs at the larger dose exceeded placebo and their own smaller dose.

Ratings of 'high' and 'good drug effect' (VAS) and desire to take the drug again rose at both larger doses above placebo and above the smaller doses (p<0.05); methamphetamine at 50 mg/70 kg produced higher 'high' ratings than the matched d-amphetamine condition (p<0.05). Values appear only in Figure 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Effects › Acute Effects; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Residual subjective effect at 24 h: ratings of 'content' were lower after 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine (40.7, SEM 10.0) than after placebo (54.6, 8.6) and than after every other active condition (p<0.05); no other residual subjective effect was significant.

Psychomotor performance: on the divided attention task all active conditions raised maximum tracking speed and the two 12 mg/70 kg conditions shortened mean hit latency (p<0.05); no other performance effects were significant, including on the digit-symbol task, and no residual performance effects at 24 h. Values appear only in Figure 4.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that both amphetamines dose-dependently increased self-administration under the $5 condition, but the results report only that the 50 mg/70 kg conditions exceeded placebo, with no significant step from the 12 to the 50 mg/70 kg condition described in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract claims a dose-response relation that the reported results support only as a two-point difference from placebo; Figure 2 carries the symbols but is an image.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2's legend defines a symbol for a difference from the 50 mg d-amphetamine condition, implying a drug difference in choice, while the text states there was no significant difference between the drugs.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether any choice comparison differed between the two amphetamines cannot be resolved from the text; the figure is an image and its symbols cannot be read.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and discussion say the two drugs did not differ on most measures, while the same results list several measures on which 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine exceeded the matched d-amphetamine condition (heart rate, 'high', stimulated, heart pounding, drug-effect-questionnaire good drug effect and drug strength), and the 12 mg/70 kg methamphetamine condition raised several ratings that the matched d-amphetamine condition did not.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary of equivalence is based on counting non-significant tests; the significant differences all point the same way (methamphetamine larger), which an equivalence claim should address.

reporting_issues.issue: Subjective ratings were analysed as sums across the session by single-factor ANOVA, cardiovascular and performance data by condition x time ANOVA, with no F statistics or degrees of freedom printed for any analysis.
reporting_issues.consequence: Degrees of freedom cannot be checked against the sample size, and the error-term inflation visible in the companion study (Hart et al., 2008) cannot be ruled in or out here.

reporting_issues.issue: The drug-effect questionnaire is described as including 'bad effects', which is never reported; Table 2 presents only items with significant effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Adverse subjective effects of either drug cannot be compared from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Pre-session urine screens were required to be negative for several drug metabolites but explicitly excluded amphetamines and THC, and no results are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Participants may have used amphetamines or cannabis between sessions; this bears directly on the 24-hour residual findings, as the authors acknowledge.

reporting_issues.issue: The claim that the $5 and $20 groups did not differ on any physiological, subjective or performance measure, which justifies pooling them (n=13), is made without reporting any test.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooling cannot be verified; with 7 and 6 participants such tests would have little power to detect a difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Three participants are said to meet criteria for current methamphetamine dependence, but the diagnostic system (DSM-IV) is not named in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the construct behind the dependence count is implicit.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3475187 (author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1 and 2 rendered as text, acknowledgements and declaration of interest read; Figures 1 to 4 are images and their values were not extracted; no supplementary files)
